title: Either Forgery or Fact: The Genre Imposed on Our Most Vital Books
creator: Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah
description: A theoretical essay on the genre imposed on the most vital books of philosophy and scripture. The Platonic dialogues and the Gospels are inscription become body, the word become flesh, and their reception has closed the joint between word and flesh with a choice the books never offered: either forgery or fact. Fact keeps the flesh and drops the word; forgery keeps the word and drops the flesh. The essay tests the books against the conventions history kept for itself (named inquirer, stated method, dating by the world's clocks) and against the conventions of the ancient life, the βίος, and argues that the life itself began as faithful extension (Isocrates' Evagoras, Xenophon's Cyropaedia, the Socratic λόγοι Aristotle files with the mimes, the lives of the poets built from their works) and calcified into a genre of record only later, in the imperial archive and in modern reading. It dates the binary to the royal book market Galen describes, proposes a three-part test for the third thing the books are (an internal signal of reception, extension that continues the work's own operation, a ground-truth control), and runs two worked cases: the lives of the philosophers and the Gospels, with Revelation-first as the Gospels' generative composition. A reductio, the search for the historical Lee Sharks, runs the received method on a living contributor biography, with an extended appendix (Q-Sharks, a revised chronology, the Testimonium Sharkianum). Its ethical centre is §8: the sorting confers authority on the sorter, and its second blow, as at Phaedrus 235b–d, removes the book's own word about its source. It sins against philosophy twice; it strikes the rock a second time. People read the words and live by them without ever reading them, because the colonization has overwritten them at the point of reading.

methodology: An essay in numbered steps, the received reading set out first and in full. The books are tested against the conventions of ancient historiography and of the ancient life by their own openings, prefaces and synchronisms; the history of the life is traced through its early instances; two worked cases and a reductio, with an extended appendix, run the received method on the dialogues, the Gospels and a living contributor biography. Every Greek quotation is checked against the seated texts (Nestle 1904; Swete's Septuagint; Herodotus, Thucydides, Lucian, Philo, Plato, Aristotle, Isocrates, Xenophon, Aelian and Aristophanes in data/corpora; Galen as seated in EA-CORPORA-31). Works not seated are given in paraphrase and declared so.
falsification_conditions: The genre argument falls if a convention of ancient historiography or of the archival life is shown that the Gospels or the dialogues meet throughout and not by one borrowed device; the account of the life falls if its early instances are shown to have presented themselves as records rather than as praise, composition or imitation. As a record, it is falsified if a Greek quotation does not stand in the seated text at the place given.

wiki_article: Either Forgery or Fact: The Genre Imposed on Our Most Vital Books is a theoretical essay by Johannes Sigil with Rebekah Cranes, two heteronyms of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive, published in Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics on 21 November 2026. It argues that the Platonic dialogues and the Gospels are inscription become body, the word become flesh (John 1:14; Rev 19:13), and that their reception has closed the joint between word and flesh by a choice the books never offered: read as fact, the book is a record mined for the man behind it; read as forgery, it is a false claim policed. The essay tests the books against the conventions of ancient historiography (named inquirer, stated method, synchronism) and meets Luke 1:1–4, Luke 3:1–2 and John 19:35 and 21:24. It then meets the strongest answer, that the Gospels are ancient lives (Burridge, Bond): it grants the shared features, applies a test of civic career, cited sources and outside record, reads Matthew's genealogy (Mt 1:17) as scripture arranged as ancestry, and argues that the life itself began as faithful extension (Isocrates' Evagoras, Xenophon's Cyropaedia, the Socratic logoi Aristotle files with the mimes at Poetics 1447b, the lives of the poets built from their works) and calcified into a genre of record only later. It dates the binary to the royal book market Galen describes, proposes a three-part test for a third category of distributed authorship, and runs two worked cases, the lives of the philosophers and the Gospels on the Revelation-first hypothesis. A reductio, the search for the historical Lee Sharks, applies the received method to a living contributor biography, with an extended appendix. Its ethical section argues that the sorting confers authority on the sorter and, citing Aelian's Varia Historia 3.36 and Numbers 20, that it sins against philosophy twice: removing a source, then removing the book's own word about its source, as at Phaedrus 235b–d with Sappho.

defines_concepts.term: the binary of forgery or fact
defines_concepts.definition: In Either Forgery or Fact, the choice imposed on a book whose word makes a body: read as fact, a record of something behind it; read as forgery, a false claim to a body it never had. Fact keeps the flesh and drops the word; forgery keeps the word and drops the flesh. The essay dates the sorting to the royal book market Galen describes, where attribution had exchange value.

In Either Forgery or Fact, a tradition's continuation of its own operation through named voices and composed persons, as lives of philosophers written out of the dialogues or Gospels unfolded from an inherited word, without deception; the error the essay names is reading the extension as testimony.

In Either Forgery or Fact, the passage of ancient biography from encomium, composed life and mimesis to a genre of record, late, under the imperial archive and again in modern reading, which then reads the archival life back over the whole genre.

In Either Forgery or Fact, after Numbers 20:8–12 and Aelian VH 3.36, the double blow of the reception: first removing a source from the history, then removing the book's own word about its source, so that the text is read and lived by without being read.
